content: Each year, approximately 6 million children under the age of 5 die globally. This loss has a profound impact on their countries, resulting in an estimated 20% reduction in adult productivity. Health services, healthcare workers, and community providers play a critical role in fostering the development of young children. The early years of a child’s life are of paramount importance for their overall development. This period represents a window of immense opportunity but also a time of vulnerability to adverse influences. Many children fail to reach their full developmental potential due to living in extreme poverty, particularly in developing countries. These children often lack adequate nutrition, care, and opportunities for learning. However, interventions can help these children and their families. Good nutrition, proper healthcare, consistent loving care, and encouragement to learn during early childhood significantly improve outcomes. Children who receive these supports perform better in school, enjoy better health, achieve higher earnings, and contribute more actively to society. This is especially crucial for children living in poverty. A strong foundation in the early years has lasting effects, influencing not only adulthood but also providing the next generation with a better start. The Care for Child Development package includes several components: Simple recommendations for healthcare workers to guide families in improving child development. Training materials for healthcare workers and community providers. Support for families to address common challenges in providing quality care for young children. Advocacy materials to promote awareness. A framework for monitoring and evaluation. The World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF, in collaboration with various partners, have developed this package to assist families in promoting the development of young children through health services, healthcare workers, and community providers. This initiative aligns with the Millennium Development Goals, emphasizing the importance of early childhood development in reducing poverty and improving societal outcomes. A 2007 Lancet series on early childhood development estimated that over 200 million children in developing countries—more than one-third of all children—fail to reach their developmental potential. The primary reasons for this disadvantage are poor nutrition and limited learning opportunities, often stemming from poverty. The WHO’s Commission on the Social Determinants of Health highlights the critical role of early childhood development in achieving equity, improving adult health, and enhancing productivity. There is robust evidence demonstrating that: Brain development is most rapid during the early years of life. Deficiencies in stimulation, support, and nurturing during this period can severely impair child development. The negative effects of early disadvantage can be mitigated. Early interventions for disadvantaged children lead to improvements in survival, health, growth, and cognitive and social development. Children who receive support in their early years achieve greater success in school. Investments in early childhood development yield significant returns. For every dollar spent on early interventions, the return on investment can be 4 to 5 times the amount, and in some cases, even higher. The healthcare system has a unique opportunity to support early childhood development. Health services often reach more young children and their families than other services, particularly through home-visiting programs. Additionally, good nutrition and health are essential for children’s development. Health services and community health activities must leverage their unique position to strengthen families’ efforts in promoting child development. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) emphasizes the obligation of all countries to enable children to reach their full potential and to support families in this process. The CRC advocates for children’s rights to development in addition to survival. Consequently, healthcare systems must aim to improve both growth and development for all children. There is now substantial evidence on how children’s development can be promoted through healthcare-related activities in developing countries. The Care for Child Development intervention is based on the best available evidence and incorporates the latest research on critical caregiver skills, such as sensitivity and responsiveness, which are essential for healthy growth and development. These skills can be effectively taught to caregivers. Caregivers and families are best positioned to support children’s growth and development through daily activities and interactions. However, families often need guidance to focus on the most critical activities for young children’s development, such as play and communication. The Care for Child Development approach provides this guidance, ensuring that children and families who need it most can benefit. When implemented on a large scale, this intervention has the potential to deliver significant public health and societal benefits. Educated and healthy individuals contribute to the financial and social wealth of their societies. By improving early childhood development, we invest in building a stronger, more equitable society.
